title: Valkey
description: Are the shared Valkey instances (CT 132, one per app) up, inside their memory budget and fast, and is each app getting hits? Open it after a Valkey* alert, when an app reports cache, lock or rate-limit errors, and weekly to see memory headroom.

panels.title: Instances up
panels.description: Every selected instance answers its exporter (redis_up; rule ValkeyDown: 0 for 2 minutes, severity from the host's tier, critical today). DOWN means an app has no cache, locks or rate limits (Kubeletto's core refuses to start without it). Also DOWN when the exporter itself is gone (rule TargetDown). Next: 'systemctl status valkey-server@<app>' in CT 132 and the Server log row.

panels.title: Memory of maxmemory, fullest
panels.description: The fullest selected instance's used memory over its maxmemory. Red from 95 % is rule ValkeyMemoryFull (15 minutes). Full is normal for a cache that evicts; with volatile-lru it is not when the keys without a TTL fill the cap, and writes then fail with OOM. Near 1-2 % today.

panels.title: Evictions, 1 h
panels.description: Keys Valkey deleted to make room (maxmemory reached) in the last hour. 0 is healthy here: instances are far below their cap. A cache that evicts is working as designed; for locks or rate limits an eviction means a lost key. No alert mirrors it: ValkeyMemoryFull fires before it matters.

panels.title: Hit ratio, 1 h
panels.description: Share of key lookups that found the key, over the last hour, for the selected instances together. For a cache a low ratio means it saves little; for locks and rate limits a miss is part of the protocol, so read it per instance in the Traffic row. n/a when nothing was looked up. No alert rule.

targets.expr: sum(increase(redis_keyspace_hits_total{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}[1h])) / (sum(increase(redis_keyspace_hits_total{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}[1h])) + sum(increase(redis_keyspace_misses_total{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}[1h])) > 0)

panels.title: Clients connected
panels.description: Open client connections on the selected instances (the exporter holds one per instance). The limit is 10000 each, so this is a sign of pool size, not saturation; a number that climbs without a matching load is an app leaking connections. No alert rule.

panels.title: Blocked clients
panels.description: Clients waiting on a blocking command (BLPOP and friends). Should be 0: nothing here issues blocking commands (the commands seen are GET, SET, EVAL, DEL, INCR and sorted-set calls), so a blocked client is unexpected. No alert rule.

panels.title: Connections rejected, 1 h
panels.description: Connections refused because maxclients (10000) was reached, in the last hour. Should be 0 (it is 0 since the instances started). Red at 1 or more means a runaway client. No alert rule.

panels.title: Error replies, 1 h
panels.description: Commands that returned an error in the last hour (wrong type, NOSCRIPT, OOM, permission). A handful is normal: a client asking for a script that was flushed gets NOSCRIPT and loads it. A steady stream is an app bug or the instance refusing writes. No alert mirrors it.

panels.title: Memory used, share of maxmemory
panels.description: Used memory over maxmemory for each selected instance (9121 is Kubeletto's, 96 MB; 9122 is larasrouter's, 64 MB). The dashed line is 95 %, rule ValkeyMemoryFull (15 minutes). With volatile-lru only keys that have a TTL are evicted: a line that climbs to the dashed one means keys without a TTL fill the cap and writes will fail with OOM.

panels.title: Memory used and resident
panels.description: Bytes Valkey has allocated for data (used) and the process's resident set as the OS sees it. Used drives eviction and ValkeyMemoryFull; resident is what CT 132's 256 MB must hold for both instances plus the exporters. Resident is mostly the fixed cost of the process at this small data size: the gap is not fragmentation. No alert rule.

panels.title: Evicted and expired keys per second
panels.description: Keys removed because memory ran out (evicted) and because their TTL ran out (expired, the normal lifecycle). Evicted should stay 0 while instances sit far below maxmemory; expired follows the apps' TTLs. No alert rule.

panels.title: Traffic and latency: rate, errors, duration
Commands per second
panels.description: Commands the apps run per second on each instance, without the exporter's own scrape commands (INFO, CONFIG GET, LATENCY and SLOWLOG calls, about 0.27 a second per instance, which would otherwise be most of the quiet instance's traffic). Its PING (one per scrape) cannot be told from an app's and stays in. A flat zero while the app runs means it cannot reach Valkey. No alert rule.

panels.title: Mean command time
panels.description: Time Valkey spends executing an average application command, from its own duration counter (queueing and the network are not included). Tens to a hundred microseconds is normal here (Lua scripts cost most); a line that climbs to milliseconds means a slow command (see the p99 panel), a big key or a CPU-starved CT. A gap is a window with no commands. No alert rule.

targets.expr: sum by (port) (rate(redis_commands_duration_seconds_total{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port", cmd!~"info|config\\|get|latency\\|.*|slowlog\\|.*|auth|client\\|.*"}[$__rate_interval])) / (sum by (port) (rate(redis_commands_total{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port", cmd!~"info|config\\|get|latency\\|.*|slowlog\\|.*|auth|client\\|.*"}[$__rate_interval])) > 0)

panels.title: p99 latency, per command
panels.description: 99th percentile of each main command's latency, from Valkey's latency histogram, per instance. With a few calls per window it is close to the slowest call: single-digit microseconds for GET, SET and DEL, about a hundred for EVAL (Lua). Taken per command because the histogram cannot be summed across commands (its buckets are sparse). A gap is a command that did not run in the window. No alert rule.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (port, cmd, le) (rate(redis_commands_latencies_usec_bucket{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port", cmd=~"get|set|del|eval|evalsha"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Keyspace hit ratio, by instance
panels.description: Share of key lookups that found the key, per instance. Read it against what the instance is for: larasrouter's reads almost always hit; Kubeletto's runs lower (about 80 % since the instance started). A sudden fall for a cache is a flush or a TTL set too short. A gap is a window with no lookups. No alert rule.

targets.expr: sum by (port) (rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}[$__rate_interval])) / (sum by (port) (rate(redis_keyspace_hits_total{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}[$__rate_interval])) + sum by (port) (rate(redis_keyspace_misses_total{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}[$__rate_interval])) > 0)

panels.title: Failed and rejected commands per second
panels.description: Failed = the command ran and returned an error (NOSCRIPT after a script flush, a wrong key type). Rejected = refused before running (OOM when maxmemory is full of non-evictable keys, a permission error). Failed at a trickle is normal; rejected above 0 is the real symptom of ValkeyMemoryFull. No alert rule.

panels.title: Clients connected and blocked
panels.description: Open connections per instance (limit 10000) and clients stuck in a blocking call. Connected tracks the apps' pool sizes: a steady number is normal, a ramp with no extra load is a leak. Blocked should be 0. No alert rule.

panels.title: New and rejected connections per second
panels.description: Connections opened per second (the exporter opens one per scrape, 0.03 a second) and connections refused at maxclients. A high accepted rate means clients connect per request instead of pooling. Rejected should be 0. No alert rule.

panels.title: Keys, and keys without a TTL
panels.description: Keys in all databases and how many of them never expire. The keyspace is tiny and short-lived here (single digits, up to 11 in a week), so 0 is common. Keys without a TTL are the ones volatile-lru cannot evict: many of them is how ValkeyMemoryFull happens. No alert rule.

targets.expr: sum by (port) (redis_db_keys{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}) - sum by (port) (redis_db_keys_expiring{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"})

panels.title: Instances and persistence
panels.description: One row per instance: which port it listens on, its eviction policy, memory used and maxmemory, whether the last RDB save succeeded, whether AOF is on, writes since the last save, and uptime. Persistence is off by design: changes since the last save only grows and AOF is off, because the instances hold no data that cannot be rebuilt (a CT rebuild is always safe). Uptime resets to 0 at a restart.

targets.expr: max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) ((redis_memory_used_bytes{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}) * on (port) group_left (tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) (redis_instance_info{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}))

max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) ((redis_memory_max_bytes{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}) * on (port) group_left (tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) (redis_instance_info{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}))

max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) ((redis_rdb_last_bgsave_status{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}) * on (port) group_left (tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) (redis_instance_info{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}))

max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) ((redis_aof_enabled{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}) * on (port) group_left (tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) (redis_instance_info{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}))

max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) ((redis_rdb_changes_since_last_save{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}) * on (port) group_left (tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) (redis_instance_info{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}))

max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) ((redis_uptime_in_seconds{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}) * on (port) group_left (tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) max by (port, tcp_port, maxmemory_policy) (redis_instance_info{job="service", instance="valkey", port=~"$port"}))

panels.title: Valkey: errors and warnings
panels.description: Lines from CT 132's journal (valkey-server@<app> units) that the journal marks warning or worse, or that mention an error or an out-of-memory refusal. Start-up notes (RDB load, 'Ready to accept connections') are normal and are not shown; a refusal or repeated warnings are the story behind a ValkeyMemoryFull or ValkeyDown. Not checked by --verify-live.

targets.expr: _stream:{_HOSTNAME="valkey"} (level:(error or critical or warning) or error or OOM)
